<!-- page 1327 -->
Payment to Henry Smyth, of $5,462 50, Compensation for Loss owing to non-acceptance of Tender for Supplies
in 1881.

AUDIT OFFICE, OTTAWA,
August 28, 1908.

SIR, - I enclose herewith copies of correspondence with the Department of Indian Affairs in reference to a payment
made by that Department out of Letter-of-Credit to the Sovereign Bank of Canada, Attorney, for $5,462.50 to
compensate Henry Smyth for loss owing to non-acceptance of his tender for Indian supplies in 1881.

I took exception to the payment on the ground that there was no Parliamentary authority for the same and suggested
that an item should be placed in the Supplementary Estimates to cover the amount. This apparently has not been done
and I am, therefore, unable to allow the amount to be charged in the appropriation accounts.

I am referring the matter to the Treasury Board as required by Sec. 60 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, and
have to request that the Board determine in what manner this item shall be entered in the appropriation accounts.

I am, Sir,
your obedient servant,

The Secretary, Treasury Board.

J. FRASER,
A.G.AUDIT OFFICE, OTTAWA,
Nov. 21, 1907.

SIR, - Manitoba and North West cheque No. 32, for the current fiscal year, is for a payment of $5,462.50 to Henry
Smyth for 'Compensation for loss amounting to $2,500.00 together with interest at 6 per cent ($2,962.50) for 19 years
and 9 months from the 1st January, 1887, to the 31st March, 1907, owing to non-acceptance of tender for Indian
supplies in 1881.' The following note is appended to the voucher in support of this payment - 'Provided for in the
Supplementary Estimates, 1907 - 08, under General Expenses for Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the North-west
Territories, Vote No. 483.'

Kindly give me a full explanation of this payment. I cannot for a moment consider that this item has been sanctioned
by Parliament, as the estimate in question reads simply 'To provide a further amount for General Expenses'. On
account of the peculiar nature of this claim and the long standing of the same, I think that Parliament is entitled to full
explanation of the same before being asked to sanction it. I think that this claim should be a special item in the
estimates to be presented to Parliament at the coming Session. In the meantime, kindly obtain an Order-in-Council
authorizing this payment, and at the same time give me a full explanation of the same.

I am,
Sir, your obedient servant,

The Deputy Sup. Indian Affairs.

J. FRASER, A.G.DEPT.
OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, OTTAWA,
Jan. 7, 1908.

SIR, - I have to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 21st November last regarding the payment to Mr. Henry
Smyth of $5,462.50 for 'Compensation for loss amounting to $2,500.00 together with interest at 6 per cent. ($2,962.50
for 19 years and 9 months from the 1st January, 1887, to the 31st March, 1907, owing to non-acceptance of tender for
Indian supplies in 1881.' In reply I beg to attach the complete explanation of the payment which was before Council
when the item was passed for insertion in the Estimates and before the House while in Committee of Supply.

<!-- page 1328 -->
Your obedient servant,

The Auditor General.

J.D. MCLEAN,
Secretary,

<!-- page 1329 -->
SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES, DEPT. OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, 1907 - 08.

Manitoba and the North-west Territories.

To provide an amount $2,500.00 with interest ($2,962.50) for nineteen years and nine months from the 1st July, 1887,
to 31st March, 1907, to compensate Henry Smyth for loss owing to the non-acceptance of his tender for Indian supplies
in 1881 $5,462.50

The claim of Mr. Smyth for compensation for loss as above stated was thoroughly examined in 1899 by Reginald
Rimmer, then Law Clerk of the Department, who recommended that $2,500 with interest, should be allowed in full
settlement of the claim. The facts are that in 1881 Mr. Smyth having forwarded his tender for Indian supplies in the
North West Territories, it was accepted; but afterwards for some reason not now apparent he withdrew his tender after
having incurred expenses, by reason of the acceptance, amounting to $4,500. In 1887 Sir John Macdonald agreed to
pay him $2,500, with interest in full settlement; and in 1894 Sir John Thompson renewed the promise. However these
arrangements were frustrated as both the Premiers died before their promises could be implemented. In view of these
facts and from the finding of the officer above mentioned it is proposed to pay this claim with interest.

See precis on following page.

Henry Smyth's Claim arising out of his tender for Indian Supplies in 1881.

Precise of Mr. Reginald Rimmer's Report, dated 12th July, 1899.

The claim presented on the part of Mr. Smyth is that in 1881 he tendered for Indian supplies in the North West
Territories, that his tender was the lowest; that it was accepted by the then Superintendent General, Sir John A.
Macdonald; that after acceptance he withdrew his tender at the request of the Superintendent General and upon the
latter's agreement to repay Mr. Smyth's actual expenditure incurred in making arrangements to carry out the contract
and a reasonable sum for damages to be subsequently agreed upon, that from 1882 to 1887 Mr. Smyth was unable to
press his claim as he was a member of Parliament during that period, that in 1887 a claim for $4,588.15 was presented
by Mr. Smyth as the amount of damages he alleged that he had suffered; that after protracted negotiations with Sir
John MacDonald he in 1887 and again in 1890 agreed that the Government should pay to Mr. Smyth $2,500 in
settlement of his claim and that he would have a sum put in the Estimates for the purpose; but this arrangement was
not fulfilled owing to the death and illness of Sir John MacDonald; that in 1894 Sir John Thompson, then Premier,
inquired into Mr. Smyth's claim and renewed Sir John MacDonald's agreement to pay $2,500 and further agreed to pay
interest on this sum at 6 per cent per annum, from 1887; that Sir John Thompson died before effect could be given to
his agreement by the amount being placed in the Estimates. Mr. Rimmer found that the real question to be decided was
not whether payment of the claim could possibly be avoided upon legal ground, but whether the tender was accepted
and the arrangements for its cancellation and subsequently for the payment of a consideration were in fact made.
There is no doubt that Mr. Smyth tendered, and there is good reason to believe that his tender was accepted. There is
evidence to show and it is considered reasonable to believe that Mr. Smyth's tender was withdrawn at the request of Sir
John MacDonald upon the terms of the agreement alleged by Mr. Smyth. The evidence consists of statutory
declarations from persons who were aware of the circumstances. There is also evidence to show that in 1887 Sir John
MacDonald offered to compromise the claim at $2,500 in full. Statutory declarations corroborate Mr. Smyth's
testimony in regard to the terms of compromise. There is nothing in the Department to contradict the declarations,
whereas the papers bear out the contention of the claimant. The Declaration fyled contain evidence that Sir John
Thompson promised to pay $2,500 and interest from 1887. A fyle of the Department

<!-- page 1330 -->
shows that Mr. Daly, as Superintendent General, decided not to admit the claim, and that Sir John Thompson
concurred in the decision after he had gone over all the papers. 'This decision was reached in February 1893, and it
does not follow that Sir John Thompson did not prior to his death in December, 1894 subsequently determine to settle
the claim upon the basis alleged. The declarations fyled tend to show that his decision was reached within a short time
prior to his death'. As all Mr. Smyth's papers bearing on his claim were handed to the Hon. J.C. Patterson, who was to
interest himself in the matter, which papers were lost or mislaid while in his possession, Mr. Rimmer suggested that
Mr. Patterson be asked concerning his knowledge of the transaction in which it is alleged he took part, and 'that unless
he is able to produce all letters and papers left with him by Mr. Smyth ...................... Parliament be asked to vote
$2,500 or such additional sum, if any, as the Minister decides should be allowed for interest, in full settlement.' On
submission of the matter to Mr. Patterson he was unable to produce the papers, but corroborated the main facts as set
forth in the evidence submitted by Mr. Smyth.

AUDIT OFFICE,
OTTAWA,
January 20, 1908.

SIR, - I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 7th instant (file No. 39,593) in reply to mine of November
21st last, regarding a payment of $5,462.50 to Mr. Henry Smyth for 'compensation for loss together with interest,
owing to non-acceptance of tender for Indian supplies in 1881.' After perusal of your letter I find that I am unable to
recede from the position taken by me in my letter of November 21st last, viz., that this claim should be made a special
item in the estimates presented to Parliament. I have, therefore, to request that a specific vote for this claim be asked
from Parliament during the current fiscal year, as unless this amount is so voted, I shall be unable to allow it to be
included in the Appropriation Accounts for the current fiscal year.

I am, Sir,
your obedient servant,

The Secretary, Dept. of Indian Affairs.

J. FRASER, A.G.
